title: My husband takes his mom's side over mine
summary: When your husband takes his mom's side, the fight is rarely about his mom. What is really happening, and what to ask for instead of loyalty.
body_markdown:
His mother said something at dinner. Small. The kind of remark that sounds like nothing if you write it down later, and lands like a slap if you were the one it was aimed at. You looked across the table at your husband. He looked at his plate.


Then in the car he said you were being sensitive. Or he said, *that's just how she is* . Or the one that really does it: *can you please just let it go.*


So here is the honest answer to the question underneath the one you searched. Him agreeing with his mother is usually not the wound. The wound is that in the four seconds when something was happening to you, he wasn't there. And when you came back for him afterward, in private, where it cost him nothing, he still wasn't there.


## Is he choosing her, or is he avoiding a fight with her?


These look identical from where you're sitting. They are not the same problem and they don't respond to the same thing.


In the first version, he actually agrees with her. In his read of the situation you are the newer person, she is the permanent one, and her opinion of how a household should run carries a weight yours doesn't. He may never say this out loud. He might not know he thinks it.


In the second version, he knows she was out of line. He just did the math on who is cheaper to disappoint, and the answer was you. Not because you matter less to him. Because you're the one who forgives him. She isn't. She'd sulk for three weeks and he'd hear about it from his sister. So he spends your goodwill instead of hers, over and over, and calls it keeping the peace. This is[conflict avoidance pointed at the safest available target](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-avoid-hard-conversations) , and the safest available target is his wife.


You can usually tell which one you're in by asking him, calmly, on a Tuesday, nowhere near a family event: what did you actually think of what she said? The man in version one defends her. The man in version two says *yeah, that wasn't okay* , and then still does nothing about it. Those need different conversations.


## The part couples are always surprised by


In Maia conversations about in-laws, the moment that keeps happening is this: the husband, hearing his wife describe the dinner, is genuinely startled. He'll say something like, *I wasn't taking her side, I just didn't think it was worth blowing up Sunday over.* He believes that. He also has no idea that his wife has been sitting alone in every one of those rooms for nine years.


The other thing we notice: within about five minutes, almost nobody is still talking about the mother-in-law. One of them brings up a completely different night, years back, when nobody said anything either. That's the actual fight. His mother is just where it happens to be visible.


## Ask him for something he can do on Sunday


"Back me up" is a feeling, not an instruction. He can agree to it sincerely and then not do it, because nothing was ever specified. Give him something with edges:


- **One sentence, in the room, at the time.** Not a confrontation. "Mom, that's not fair to her," and then pass the potatoes. The content matters far less than the fact that you weren't alone for those four seconds.
- **He raises things with her, not you.** If a boundary needs setting with his mother, it is his job. A wife delivering it is a wife picking a fight with her mother-in-law. A son delivering it is a family sorting itself out.
- **Decide together before you go, not in the car after.** What's off limits, what you'll do if it comes up, what the exit looks like. This is the same work as[deciding whose family you spend the holidays with](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/fighting-about-whose-family-for-the-holidays) : it goes fine when it's a plan and badly when it's improvised in front of an audience.
- **Name the repair you want afterward.** Some people need the apology. Some need him to text his mother that night. Say which.


## The moves that make him dig in


Making him rank you is the big one. "It's her or me" gets you a defense of his mother almost every time, because you've asked a question no decent son can answer the way you want. Building the case is the other one: arriving with a list of eleven incidents going back to the wedding. Every item you add gives him something to argue with, and by number four he's defending his childhood instead of hearing you.


Going after his mother directly, to force him to pick, tends to hand him the moral high ground he was looking for. And waiting for him to notice on his own is not a strategy, it's just more Sundays.


## When you've said it clearly and nothing moves


If you have named this plainly, more than once, without an ultimatum, and a year later you're still absorbing the same remarks in the same chair, the problem has changed shape. It isn't a misunderstanding anymore. It's a decision he keeps making.


That's worth looking at directly, because it tends to show up elsewhere too: in whose comfort gets protected, in whose version of events gets believed, in how much of your marriage is[performed for other people](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/pretending-everything-is-fine-in-front-of-family) . A partner who consistently treats your hurt as the manageable cost is telling you something about the marriage, not about his mother. Being told for years that[your reaction is the problem](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/my-partner-dismisses-my-feelings) wears down your sense of what's reasonable, and it's worth checking that with someone outside it.


Most of the time, though, this is something much more ordinary. A man who never learned how to disappoint his mother, married to a woman who has quietly agreed to be disappointed instead. That's fixable, but only once it's said out loud in words he can act on.


If you're trying to work out which version you're living in, or what you'd even ask for if he agreed to change something, it can help to talk the whole thing through first, before the next visit. Maia can walk through your specific situation with you, or with both of you, and help you find the one sentence you actually need him to say.
